newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Central Bank under fire over bond fraud.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Central Bank under fire over bond fraud.

text.p: As a parliamentary probe into a multi-million-dollar bond scam continued, Brazil's Central Bank on Tuesday found itself once again in the line of fire.

Newspapers reported that one of the main conduits for illicit gains from the alleged racket, the Banco do Estado de Rondonia (Beron), was being run by the Central Bank at the time. "How is it that a bank under federal intervention could be used as the launderer of dirty money?" asked political columnist Dora Kramer in the daily Jornal do Brasil.

The municipal bond scandal, which has echoes of the corruption probe that toppled President Fernando Collor de Mello in 1992, has dominated local media for weeks. Its most recent target was Celso Pitta, mayor of Brazil's largest city, Sao Paulo, who is being probed by police and tax authorities.

Senators heading a Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry say brokers and officials siphoned off millions of dollars through suspect state and municipal bond issues. States sold their debt at below market price to friendly brokerages, which in turn passed the securities on for a considerable profit.
The ill-gotten rewards were reportedly sitting in secret bank accounts in Paraguay and the Caribbbean.
No one was available for comment at the Central Bank but officials have defended the institution by pointing out it advised the Senate against authorising the debt issues.

Brasilia University political scientist David Fleischer said the bank had partially covered itself by having the Senate give final approval for the operations. "The authorisation is one thing. What about the hanky panky that goes on afterwards? Something will obviously have to be done about the Central Bank's supervision (of the banking system)," Fleischer said.

With regard to Beron, the Central Bank has said it was the first to suspect the bank's Sao Paulo branch was being used as the control centre for a huge money laundering operation. But political analysts believe someone will have to pay for slack auditing of the financial system.
Senators, who frequently vent their wrath on the Central Bank, have been calling for the head of its public debt department, Jaire da Cruz Ferreira, to be fired.
Last week, resignation rumours that periodically dog Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola, a technocrat who dislikes the limelight, resurfaced. The rumours were promptly denied.

"We may well see Loyola go once the dust has settled. I think (Central Bank Director of Controls Claudio) Mauch will have to leave too," Fleischer said. "The bank's supervision of the market has been letting people get away with murder."
